name: ラ・ランコントル (La Rencontre)

claims.text: No information on cross-contamination controls is publicly available. French omakase kitchens share all preparation surfaces; wheat flour is used in pastry, sauces, and bread — standard cross-contact risk applies.
No specific mention of soy sauce use, but modern French-Japanese fusion techniques may incorporate wheat-containing soy sauce. This cannot be confirmed or ruled out without direct inquiry.
All courses include fish and meat components; butter, cream, and eggs are central to classic French technique. Vegan cross-contact in a shared kitchen is unavoidable without specific accommodation.

The restaurant explicitly asks guests to notify in advance of any food intolerances or allergies ('苦手な食材やアレルギーがございましたら、必ず事前にお申し付けください'). Same-day requests cannot be accommodated as ingredients are sourced the morning of service.
Advance allergy communication is built into the reservation process; the chef personally sources all ingredients, which may allow for substitutions when arranged well ahead of time.

name: ラ・トスカ (La Tosca (Osteria La Tosca))

claims.text: Pasta and pizza are staple menu items; wheat flour is central to the kitchen. Cross-contamination from pasta water and shared surfaces is a near-certainty in a small six-table kitchen. No gluten-free alternatives are listed.
No soy-sauce-based dishes are listed on the Italian menu, but soy sauce with wheat is not the primary concern here — pasta and pizza dough are the principal gluten sources.
Meat, seafood, cheese, and butter are used throughout the menu. Shared pans and surfaces make vegan cross-contact highly likely in a small kitchen with no stated vegan protocols.

No information about allergy handling protocols was found on any source. Given the small size and cash-only, no-reservations-required format, advance phone inquiry in Japanese is strongly recommended for anyone with celiac disease or severe allergies.

name: MACCHA HOUSE 抹茶館 善光寺仲見世通り店 (Maccha House Zenkoji Nakamise-dori)

claims.text: No information about cross-contamination controls is published. The kitchen produces tiramisu (wheat-containing sponge/ladyfinger), soft serve, and shaved ice in a compact two-floor café setup — shared equipment is very likely.
No soy sauce is used in a matcha dessert menu, but wheat appears structurally in tiramisu and parfait components (sponge cake / ladyfingers). No allergen sheet is published online.
Dairy is pervasive across the menu (mascarpone, soft-serve ice cream, milk for lattes). No non-dairy alternatives are offered, so vegan cross-contact is unavoidable.
The official store page states only 'for details, please inquire with staff' — no written allergen matrix or dedicated allergy protocol is described.

No gluten-free handling information is published. A traditional kaiseki kitchen uses wheat-based soy sauce throughout multiple courses; cross-contamination is a structural risk rather than an exception.
Standard Japanese kaiseki cuisine uses koikuchi soy sauce (wheat-containing) in marinades, dipping sauces, and simmered dishes. No tamari or GF soy sauce option is advertised.
Fish-based dashi (katsuobushi, niboshi) is the foundation of traditional kaiseki seasoning and is present in nearly every course. No plant-based dashi alternative is advertised.
No allergen menu or allergy-handling protocol is published. The Nagano CVB listing notes English menus are available, but makes no mention of dietary accommodation procedures.
English menus are available, which may ease communication of dietary needs.

The soba restaurant is an active niko-hachi (80% buckwheat / 20% wheat flour) kitchen. Wheat flour is handled continuously throughout service, making cross-contamination unavoidable for celiac or wheat-allergic diners.
The tsuyu (dipping sauce and hot broth) is made with soy sauce, which in standard Japanese production contains wheat. No wheat-free soy sauce alternative is mentioned.
Katsuobushi (bonito), sodabushi (striped jack mackerel), and sabobushi (mackerel) are used in the soba tsuyu. Tempura is a menu centerpiece. No plant-based broth option is offered.

The Nagano Tourism Board listing notes that 'allergy-friendly options and religious dietary requirements are available upon consultation' — but this appears to reflect general tourist-facing language rather than a documented allergy protocol.
No preservatives or food additives (防腐剤など添加物不使用) are used in any products, including the noodles and tsuyu ingredients.
Buckwheat is sourced exclusively from named contracted farms in Nagano Prefecture and stone-milled, providing full ingredient traceability for the noodles themselves.
Panko-breaded tonkatsu and tempura are core menu items, meaning wheat flour and breadcrumbs are in active use throughout service. Cross-contamination with soba and rice dishes must be assumed.
Standard Japanese soy sauce (shoyu) containing wheat is used in soba broth and likely in all savory preparations. No tamari or wheat-free soy sauce is mentioned anywhere.
Animal products — pork, duck, herring, egg, and fish-based dashi — are present in virtually every dish. There is no plant-only preparation pathway available.

No allergy handling policy, allergen chart, or staff allergy communication procedure is documented on any platform reviewed. Diners with wheat allergy or serious dietary restrictions should call ahead: 026-232-5776.

name: Wafu no Yado Masuya (和風の宿 ますや)

claims.text: Shared ryokan kitchen with standard wheat-containing kaiseki components; no documented GF protocol — assume cross-contact and pre-confirm every course.
Standard kaiseki uses wheat shoyu and barley/wheat miso; per seed the kitchen can swap in a gluten-free miso for celiac guests on request — confirm tamari for shoyu too.
Kaiseki is fish/dashi-based; no vegan menu published — arrange directly if needed.
Per seed, celiac-attentive on advance request — GF miso and GF tempura alternatives across a careful multi-course meal; not a published program, so book direct and confirm.
Best (near-only) celiac dinner+breakfast option at the snow-monkey base; willing to accommodate gluten-free with advance arrangement.

name: 麺道 麒麟児 大門店 (Mendo Kirinji Daimon-ten)

claims.text: No dedicated gluten-free preparation area or fryer documented. Wheat noodles are the core product; cross-contamination is a near-certainty.
Standard shoyu tare is used in the 中華そば; Japanese soy sauce typically contains wheat. No tamari or GF soy sauce alternative is mentioned.
Every broth on the menu is chicken- or duck-based. No plant-based broth or topping alternatives have been documented.
